title: From Adam to Edom
sum: Chronicles opens with the whole human race. In fifty-four verses it boils down Genesis 5, 10, 11, 25 and 36: from Adam to Noah, the seventy nations descended from Noah's sons, the line of Shem to Abraham, then Abraham's sons by Hagar and Keturah, Isaac's sons, and the clans, kings and chiefs of Edom. There are no stories, no ages and almost no comments; the reader is expected to know Genesis.

The order matters. Each time, the side branches come first and the line that leads to Israel last: Japheth and Ham before Shem, Ishmael and Keturah's sons before Isaac, Esau before Israel. By the end of the chapter the stage is clear for the twelve sons of Israel in chapter 2. Israel's story begins with Adam, inside the family of all nations.
readings: Read as a family tree

On this reading the chapter is what it looks like: an index of Genesis, showing where Israel came from. The names are mostly the same as in Genesis, with small spelling differences that come from copying (Diphath for Riphath, 1:6). The Chronicler had the Torah in front of him and shortened it.
Read as a statement of faith

On this reading the bare list makes a claim: the God of Israel is the God of all peoples, and Israel's history is part of human history. Beginning with Adam, rather than with Abraham or Moses, says the same thing Genesis says, that every nation comes from one family. Israel was small and under Persian rule when this was written; its genealogy still started at the beginning of the world.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as a faithful abstract of Genesis, made by Ezra or a scribe of his time (Bava Batra 15a), to introduce the history of David's house.
views.C: Critical scholars agree the Chronicler drew directly on Genesis, close to the Masoretic form. The selection, which follows Genesis' own pattern of side lines first and main line last, is the Chronicler's way of placing the returned community among the nations.
views.S: This chapter draws on Genesis rather than Samuel–Kings. It copies most of Genesis 10 word for word but drops the narrative remarks on Nimrod's kingdom, the cities of Canaan and the nations' languages, keeping only "he was the first to become a hero on the earth" (1:10).
views.J: The Talmud asks why Scripture bothers to say that Timna was Lotan's sister (1:39). It answers that she was a princess who wanted to join Abraham's family, was turned away, and became the concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz and the mother of Amalek (1:36; Genesis 36:12): a warning against pushing away those who seek to join Israel (Bavli Sanhedrin 99b).
views.X: Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs the same line backward to "Adam, son of God" (Luke 3:38), and its names from Adam to Abraham match 1:1–4 and 1:24–27 (except for Luke's extra Cainan). Christian readers see in both the universal reach of the gospel.

deep.b:
Genesis is built on the phrase "these are the generations of" (toledot). Chronicles keeps the order of Genesis but cuts away almost everything except the names:

Adam to Noah's sons (1:1–4) from Genesis 5. The nations (1:5–23) from Genesis 10, Japheth, Ham, Shem. Shem to Abraham (1:24–27) from Genesis 11:10–26. Abraham's sons (1:28–34): Ishmael's twelve (Genesis 25:12–16), Keturah's (Genesis 25:1–4) and Isaac's (Genesis 25:19–26). Esau and Seir (1:35–54) from Genesis 36: Esau's sons, the Horite clans of Seir, the kings of Edom and the chiefs.

The pattern "side branch first, chosen line last" is Genesis' own. It means that the chapter ends with Edom, Israel's brother, just before Israel himself appears (2:1).

echoes: Genesis 5:1–32; Genesis 10:1–32; Genesis 11:10–26; Genesis 25:1–26; Genesis 36:1–43; Luke 3:23–38

settings.what: From Adam to the sons of Israel
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud), the Chronicler's first readers
settings.when: Written after the return from Babylon (most scholars: about 400–300 BC); the names run from Adam to the kings and chiefs of Edom
settings.why: To place Israel inside the whole human family from Adam, and then to narrow the line, through Shem, Abraham and Isaac, to Israel. The nations are not left out; they are listed first. For a small people under Persia, the list said that they had a place in God's plan for the world from the start.

title: Judah's Family
sum: Israel's twelve sons are named in one verse (2:1–2), and then the writer turns at once to Judah. Judah's line includes a Canaanite wife, a dead firstborn, Tamar's twins and, from Perez, the line of Hezron. Through Ram it runs to Boaz, Jesse and David, the seventh son (2:9–17). Through Caleb and Jerahmeel, Hezron's other sons, it spreads into the clans and towns of the south: Hebron, Bethlehem, Kiriath-jearim, Ziph.

Woven into the list are outsiders: Canaanite Bath-shua, an Ishmaelite father, an Egyptian slave who marries his master's daughter, the Kenites and the Rechabites. Judah, the royal tribe, is a family that took others in. Its first story is a warning: Er was evil and died, and Achar "acted unfaithfully," the word Chronicles will later use for the sin that led to exile (9:1).
readings: Read as clan records

Many scholars think much of this chapter comes from old records of the clans and villages of the Judean hills and the Negev. "Father of" a town often means its founder or leading family (2:42), and the lists map who lived where. Some of these groups, such as the Calebites and Jerahmeelites, were once separate from Judah (1 Samuel 27:10; 30:29).
Read as the road to David

On this reading the chapter is built around David (2:15), who stands at its center, surrounded by Hezron's other descendants. The line from Perez to David is the same as Ruth 4:18–22, and the writer pauses for no one else in it. Everything in Judah's family is arranged around the king to come.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as the record of Judah's families from Genesis, Ruth and the clans' own registers, with David as its goal. Jewish tradition identified many of the names with heroes known elsewhere.
views.C: Critical scholars see in the chapter layers of older clan lists, some from before the monarchy, joined into a single tree by the Chronicler. The differences with Samuel (David as seventh son, 2:15; Abigail's husband an Ishmaelite, 2:17) show the Chronicler used sources beyond Samuel.
views.S: David is the seventh son here but the eighth in 1 Samuel 16:10–11 and 17:12. Amasa's father Jether is an Ishmaelite here and an Israelite in the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 17:25, where he is called Ithra. Chronicles evidently had information beyond the Samuel text we know.
views.J: The rabbis read the names as titles of virtue. Bezalel (2:20) was the craftsman of the tabernacle, and Hur his grandfather was said to have been killed for resisting the golden calf (Bavli Sanhedrin 7a). The "clans of scribes" at Jabez (2:55) were taken as disciples of Torah.
views.X: Matthew 1:3–6 follows this chapter closely: Judah, Tamar, Perez, Hezron, Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, David. Matthew adds Rahab and Ruth as the mothers, so Tamar is joined by two more foreign women in Jesus' line.

deep.b:
Matthew's genealogy of Jesus begins "Abraham fathered Isaac" and copies the form of Chronicles: "X fathered Y." From Judah to David (Matthew 1:2–6) the names follow 1 Chronicles 2:1–15, in their Greek forms. Matthew's additions are the women: Tamar (as here, 2:4), Rahab, Ruth and "the wife of Uriah." Matthew's spelling Salmon follows Ruth 4:21; Chronicles has Salma (2:11). Luke's line (Luke 3:31–34) has the same names, except that the critical text of Luke (NA28), following the oldest manuscripts, has Admin and Arni where later manuscripts have Aram (Ram), and Sala for Salmon.

So the bare list of 1 Chronicles 2 became, in the Gospels, the first page of the New Testament.

echoes: Genesis 35:23–26; Genesis 38:1–30; Ruth 4:18–22; Joshua 7:1–26; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; Exodus 31:1–5; Matthew 1:1–6; Luke 3:31–34

settings.what: The genealogy of Judah and David's line
settings.by: The Chronicler, from Genesis, Ruth, Samuel and other lists
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud), most of whom were of Judah, Benjamin or Levi
settings.when: Written after the return from Babylon (most scholars: about 400–300 BC); the line of David runs past the exile to the generations after Zerubbabel (3:17–24)
settings.why: Judah comes first, and David's family is at its center. The line of David's sons is carried past the exile, which tells readers that the royal family still existed in their own day, even without a throne. The lists also include Judah's mixed roots, such as Tamar and an Egyptian slave who married into the clan (2:34–35). So belonging was not only a matter of pure descent.
views: Williamson and others: the line in chapter 3 keeps hope alive for a future king.
Others: the list honors the family without expecting it to rule again.

title: The House of David
sum: David's sons come first: six born at Hebron, each by a different mother, then thirteen at Jerusalem, four of them by Bathsheba, here called Bath-shua. Tamar is the only daughter named. Then the kings of Judah follow one per generation, Solomon to Josiah, with Josiah's four sons and Jehoiachin's (Jeconiah's) line after him.

The chapter's real surprise comes after the exile. Jeconiah, "who was taken captive," had sons in Babylon, and through Pedaiah his grandson Zerubbabel came home to rebuild the temple. The list keeps going for several generations more, down to, or near, the Chronicler's own day. The throne was gone, but David's house was still there, still counted, still waiting.
readings: Read as a royal register

The list reads like an archive of the royal family, from Hebron to the late Persian period. Its accuracy can be checked: the kings agree with Kings, Jehoiachin's sons are confirmed by Babylonian ration tablets, and Zerubbabel is known from Ezra, Haggai and Zechariah.
Read as hope

On this reading the list carries a promise. God told David his house would stand forever (17:11–14), and here, after the exile, the house still stands. The names of Zerubbabel's children, "loyal love returns," "the LORD is gracious," are prayers, and the Targum read the last name, Anani, as the Messiah.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as the line of the house of David that continued after the exile, kept by the family and the scribes. Its last generations bring the record to the time of the writer.
views.C: Critical scholars use the length of the list after Zerubbabel to date Chronicles: about six generations in the Hebrew (to about 400 BC) or more in the Greek of 3:21. Some think the list was extended by later hands.
views.S: The sons born at Hebron and Jerusalem come from 2 Samuel 3:2–5 and 5:13–16, with Chileab called Daniel and two extra sons in Jerusalem. The list of kings agrees with Kings but has nothing on how any of them reigned. Bathsheba appears with no word about Uriah.
views.J: The Targum calls Anani (3:24) "the King Messiah who is to be revealed." The rabbis taught that Jeconiah repented in prison and that God revoked the curse of Jeremiah 22:30 (Leviticus Rabbah 19:6), which allowed the line to continue in Zerubbabel.
views.X: Matthew's list of kings (Matthew 1:6–11) follows 3:5–16 but skips Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah and Jehoiakim to make three groups of fourteen. After the exile, Matthew and Luke both name Shealtiel and Zerubbabel and then go their own way. Christian readers have seen the chapter's unfinished line as pointing to Jesus, "son of David" (Matthew 1:1).

deep.h: Chronicles, Matthew and Luke on David's line
deep.b:
David to the exile. Chronicles names every king of Judah (except Athaliah) from Solomon to Zedekiah (3:10–16). Matthew follows the same royal line from Solomon but leaves out four kings (Matthew 1:8, 11). Luke does not use the royal line at all: he traces Jesus through David's son Nathan (3:5; Luke 3:31) and a series of names found nowhere in the Old Testament.

The exile. Chronicles makes Zerubbabel the son of Pedaiah (3:19); Matthew, Ezra and Haggai make him the son of Shealtiel. Luke makes Shealtiel the son of Neri, not of Jeconiah (Luke 3:27).

After Zerubbabel. Chronicles names Meshullam, Hananiah and their families. Matthew names Abiud and Luke Rhesa, neither of whom is in Chronicles. The Gospel lists go on through nine to twenty generations to Joseph.

How do the lines fit together? Since the 200s, Christians have offered answers: Julius Africanus proposed levirate marriages joining the two lines (Eusebius, Church History 1.7); later writers suggested Luke gives Mary's line. Modern scholars mostly think Matthew and Luke drew on different family traditions about David's descendants, both valued in early Christian families, and arranged them for their own purposes. Chronicles, which they both knew, is the shared Old Testament base for the names up to Zerubbabel.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the list is shaped like the temple's rebuilding
deep.b:
My own reading, offered as a guess. The line after the exile is arranged around Zerubbabel, who stands in the middle of it with his children, including a named daughter (3:19–20). The names of his children read like a liturgy of the return: "repaid" (Meshullam), "the LORD is gracious" (Hananiah), "the LORD blesses" (Berechiah), "the LORD is loyal" (Hasadiah), "loyal love returns" (Jushab-hesed). Haggai called Zerubbabel the LORD's "signet ring" (Haggai 2:23), undoing the curse on his grandfather Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24). I suspect the Chronicler placed the names this way so that the reader who reaches Zerubbabel hears, in the names of his children, the answer to Jeremiah's curse: the house of David, cast off, has been taken back.

What is already in print: that Haggai's "signet ring" reverses Jeremiah 22:24 is standard in the commentaries on Haggai (for example Meyers and Meyers), and commentators on Chronicles (Japhet, Klein, Knoppers) note the hopeful meaning of the children's names. What I add is only the suggestion that the Chronicler arranged the list itself as an answer to the curse, which I have not seen argued and cannot prove.

echoes: 2 Samuel 3:2–5; 2 Samuel 5:13–16; 2 Samuel 7:11–16; 2 Kings 24:6–17; 2 Kings 25:27–30; Jeremiah 22:24–30; Ezra 3:2; Haggai 2:23; Matthew 1:6–16; Luke 3:23–31

title: Jabez and the Clans of the South
sum: The chapter adds more of Judah's clans: Shobal's line, the families of Hur and Bethlehem, Ashhur's wives and, without warning, Jabez. His name sounds like "pain," and he prays to the God of Israel to bless him, widen his borders and keep harm away. God grants it. Then the list returns to Caleb's and Kenaz's families, the Egyptian princess Bithiah, and clans of craftsmen, linen workers and royal potters.

From 4:24 the chapter turns to Simeon, a small tribe living inside Judah's land around Beersheba. Its towns match Joshua 19, "up to the time David reigned." Two raids close it: in Hezekiah's day Simeonites took pasture near Gedor from the people of Ham and the Meunites, and others went to Seir and struck down the last of Amalek.
readings: Read as a model of prayer

Jabez stands out as a man who asked God for blessing and received it. Readers from the Targum to modern devotional books have taken him as a model: a man burdened by his name who did not accept it as his fate, but prayed. The short story fits Chronicles' theme that God answers those who call on him (5:20).
Read in its setting

Read in its place, Jabez's prayer is about land. "Widen my borders" asks for territory, and the chapter is full of clans looking for room: Simeon looking for pasture (4:39), taking land from others (4:41–43). On this reading Jabez is a clan founder whose story explains how his family came to hold more land than its neighbors.

views.H: Traditional readers see in Jabez a real man of Judah, perhaps a founder of the town named in 2:55. The Talmud and Targum identify him with Othniel and make his prayer one for Torah learning.
views.C: Critical scholars see 4:1–23 as a collection of clan notices from Judah, some very old, and 4:24–43 as Simeon's records, some from Hezekiah's time (4:41). Jabez is often read as a story that explains a name, of the kind found in Genesis.
views.S: None of this chapter is in Samuel or Kings. Simeon's town list comes from Joshua 19:2–8, and the note that the towns were Simeon's "up to the time David reigned" (4:31) fills a gap that Samuel only hints at (1 Samuel 27:6).
views.J: The rabbis taught that Jabez was Othniel, the first judge, and that his prayer was for Torah and students (Bavli Temurah 16a). They read Bithiah as the princess who rescued Moses (Bavli Megillah 13a) and 4:22 as a coded account of Ruth and her family (Bavli Bava Batra 91b).
views.X: Christian readers have long taken Jabez's prayer as an example of bold, trusting prayer. In 2000, Bruce Wilkinson's The Prayer of Jabez made it famous; many found encouragement in it, while others warned against treating it as a formula for success.

deep.h: The prayer of Jabez and its modern readers
deep.b:
Jabez's prayer has four parts: "bless me," "widen my borders," "your hand with me," "keep harm away" (4:10). In the Hebrew it is an "if" with no "then": the vow is never finished. God's answer is one line.

Older readings. The Targum and Talmud made Jabez a teacher of Torah who asked for students and learning. Medieval Jewish commentators read the prayer as a request to be spared the pain his name threatened.

The modern movement. Bruce Wilkinson's The Prayer of Jabez (2000) sold millions of copies and spawned devotionals, music and merchandise. Wilkinson urged readers to pray Jabez's words daily, asking God for more influence and ministry, and many reported answered prayers and new boldness. Critics, including evangelical scholars and pastors, said the book turned a single verse into a formula, encouraged a focus on personal success, and ignored the verse's context of land and clan. Defenders replied that Wilkinson was teaching faith in God's generosity, not a magic phrase.

What the text supports. The verse clearly presents Jabez as a man who asked and was heard. It does not tell readers to repeat his words, and its "borders" are, in context, a clan's land. Between those two points readers have room to disagree about how a story becomes a model.

echoes: Genesis 28:20–22; Genesis 3:16; Genesis 35:18; Joshua 15:16–19; Joshua 19:1–9; Exodus 2:5–10; Exodus 17:8–16; 1 Samuel 27:6

settings.when: At an unknown time in Judah's early history
settings.why: A short prayer for blessing, land and protection from harm, set in the middle of a list of names: 'And God brought about what he asked.' It turns the genealogy into a lesson that the God of Israel hears those who call on him. For readers in a small and pressed province, it was a model of asking God for room to live.

settings.what: Simeon and the tribes east of the Jordan
settings.by: The Chronicler, from tribal records, some entered in the family register when Jotham was king of Judah and Jeroboam was king of Israel (5:17)
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud)
settings.when: Written after the return from Babylon (most scholars: about 400–300 BC)
settings.why: Two notes give these lists a purpose. 5:1–2 explains why the birthright went to Joseph while the ruler came from Judah, which keeps both north and south in the family. 5:25–26 says Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh were exiled to Assyria because they 'acted unfaithfully.' For readers who knew exile, the lists taught that land is held by faithfulness and lost by unfaithfulness.

title: The Tribes Across the Jordan
sum: Reuben was the firstborn, but he lost the birthright when he slept with his father's concubine. The chapter explains: the birthright went to Joseph, and the ruler came from Judah. Reuben's clans are listed down to Beerah, deported by the Assyrian king, and Gad's and the half-tribe of Manasseh's leaders follow.

In the middle comes a war story. The eastern tribes fought the Hagrites and their Ishmaelite allies, cried out to God in the battle and won, because they trusted him. But the chapter ends with the same tribes going after other gods, and God stirring up the king of Assyria to carry them away to Halah, Habor and the river of Gozan, "to this day." Faith won them the land; unfaithfulness lost it.
readings: Read as a lesson in two halves

The chapter is a small sermon. When the eastern tribes trusted God, "he let himself be moved by their pleas" (5:20). When they "acted unfaithfully" (5:25), he sent them into exile. The Chronicler's whole history follows the same rule, and the returned exiles were meant to learn it.
Read as frontier history

On this reading the chapter preserves real memories of Israel's east-bank tribes: herds pushing toward the desert, wars with Arab tribes for pasture, the censuses of Jeroboam II's time, and the deportations of Tiglath-pileser III in 733 BC. Reuben's towns and Gad's land are known from the Moabite Stone and Assyrian records.

views.H: Traditional readers take the war with the Hagrites as a real event of Saul's time and the exile as the first stage of the Assyrian conquest, both recorded in the tribes' registers.
views.C: Critical scholars see genuine old material in the Reubenite and Gadite lists and in the Hagrite war, retold in the Chronicler's language of faith and reward. The joining of Pul and Tiglath-pileser as two names (5:26) shows the writer combining 2 Kings 15:19 and 15:29.
views.S: Kings tells of the deportation of Gilead and Galilee by Tiglath-pileser (2 Kings 15:29) and of Samaria's exile under Shalmaneser and Sargon (2 Kings 17:6). Chronicles applies the place names of the second to the first, and gives as the reason the eastern tribes' idolatry.
views.J: Jewish tradition took Reuben's sin seriously but taught that Reuben repented (Genesis Rabbah 84:19). The verse "the birthright was Joseph's" (5:2) was used to explain why Joseph's sons received two tribal portions.
views.X: Christian readers have read the Reubenites' victory through prayer as an example of faith, like the heroes of Hebrews 11 who "became mighty in war." Revelation 7:5–8 still counts Reuben and Gad among the tribes of the redeemed.

echoes: Genesis 35:22; Genesis 48:5; Genesis 49:3–4; Genesis 49:8–10; Numbers 32:1–42; Joshua 13:8–33; 2 Kings 15:19; 2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 17:6; Psalm 83:6

settings.what: The cry of the eastern tribes in battle
settings.by: Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh
settings.to: God, during the war with the Hagrites
settings.when: In the days of Saul, east of the Jordan
settings.why: The prayer is reported, not quoted. 'It was to God they had shouted in the battle, and he let himself be moved by their pleas, since they had put their trust in him.' It is the Chronicler's first example of a pattern he will repeat often: those who rely on God win. The same tribes are later exiled for unfaithfulness (5:25–26), so readers see both sides of the pattern in one chapter.

title: Levi: Priests, Singers and Towns
sum: Levi's family is at the center of the genealogies. First come the high priests, from Aaron through Zadok to Jehozadak, who went into exile (6:1–15). Then the clans of Gershom, Kohath and Merari, including the family of Samuel (6:16–30). David appointed singers from all three clans when the ark came to rest: Heman, Samuel's grandson, in the middle, Asaph on his right, Ethan on his left, each with a family tree reaching back to Levi (6:31–47).

Only Aaron's sons burn offerings and make atonement; the other Levites do the rest of the work of God's house (6:48–53). The chapter ends with the Levites' towns, forty-eight of them spread through all the tribes, from Hebron in Judah to Ramoth in Gilead (6:54–81). Worship is placed at the heart of Israel, and its servants live in every part of the land.
readings: Read as the order of worship

On this reading the chapter is a charter for the temple's staff after the exile: who could be a priest, who were the singers, and where they belonged. Its high-priest list proves that Jeshua, the high priest of the return, descended from Aaron, and its singers' genealogies show that the music of the second temple went back to David.
Read as theology in names

The chapter places Levi at the center, between the tribes of the south and the north. Its towns are scattered through every tribe, as Jacob's words said: "I will divide them among Jacob" (Genesis 49:7). On this reading the Levites hold Israel together: the people are one because their worship is one.

views.H: Traditional readers take the high-priest list as a true record, though not every high priest is listed. Samuel was a Levite who lived in Ephraim, and David truly founded the temple music.
views.C: Critical scholars see the high-priest list as an idealized line linking Zadok to Aaron, perhaps compiled after the exile. Many think Samuel's place among the Levites and the singers' long pedigrees reflect the Levites' rising status in the Persian period. The town list is closely related to Joshua 21.
views.S: Samuel and Kings never connect Samuel with Levi or David with organized temple music. Chronicles adds both. The towns of Joshua 21 appear here in a rearranged and damaged form, with Dan's towns missing and several spellings changed.
views.J: The rabbis read the high-priest list with care and noticed its gaps; Josephus gives a somewhat different list (Antiquities 10.151–153). Heman, Asaph and Jeduthun (often identified with Ethan) were counted among the ten elders whose words are in the Psalms (Bavli Bava Batra 14b–15a), and Samuel was honored as equal to Moses and Aaron (Psalm 99:6).
views.X: Hebrews contrasts Aaron's priests, who served "day after day," with Christ, a priest "in the order of Melchizedek" from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:11–17). Christian worship has drawn on David's singers for its tradition of choirs and psalmody.

deep.b:
Numbers 35:1–8 orders that the Levites receive forty-eight towns with their pastures, and Joshua 21 lists them. Chronicles' list follows Joshua with three kinds of differences.

Order. Chronicles starts with Aaron's towns (6:54–60), then gives totals for the other clans (6:61–65), then the towns by name (6:66–81). Joshua gives totals first.

Damage. Some lines have suffered in copying. Juttah (6:59), Gibeon (6:60), and two of Zebulun's towns (6:77) are missing, so the totals do not add up. Dan is missing from 6:61, and of Dan's four towns Eltekeh and Gibbethon are gone, while Aijalon and Gath-rimmon appear under Ephraim (6:69). See the variants on those verses.

Names. About a third of the names differ: Hilen for Holon, Ashtaroth for Be-eshterah, Jokmeam for Kibzaim, Kedesh for Kishion. Most are spellings; some may be later names.

Scholars disagree about the list's origin. W. F. Albright and Benjamin Mazar thought it reflected real Levite settlements of David's or Solomon's time. Others date it to Josiah's reform. Graeme Auld argued that Joshua 21 was based on an earlier form of Chronicles' list.

echoes: Exodus 6:16–25; Numbers 3:1–39; Numbers 35:1–8; Joshua 21:1–42; 1 Samuel 1:1; 1 Samuel 8:1–3; 2 Kings 25:18–21; Ezra 7:1–5; Psalm 88:1; Psalm 89:1; Hebrews 7:11–17

settings.what: The genealogy and towns of Levi
settings.by: The Chronicler, from priestly and Levitical records and Joshua 21
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud), and especially the priests and Levites serving in the second Temple
settings.when: Written after the return from Babylon (most scholars: about 400–300 BC)
settings.why: Levi stands at the center of the tribal lists. The line of high priests (6:1–15) runs to the exile, and the singers Heman, Asaph and Ethan are traced back to Levi (6:31–48). The list showed readers who had the right to serve at the altar and to sing in the Temple, and it rooted the Temple choirs in David's own appointment.

title: The Northern Tribes
sum: Six northern tribes are covered quickly: Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher, most with their fighting strength from military rolls "in David's days." Dan and Zebulun have no list of their own, though a fragment in 7:12 may be all that remains of Dan's.

Two moments break through. Zelophehad "had daughters," a reminder of the five sisters who won the right to inherit. And Ephraim lost his sons in a cattle raid on Gath, mourned many days, and named a new son Beriah, "in trouble." From that son of grief came Joshua son of Nun, who led Israel into the land. A daughter, Sheerah, built three towns.
readings: Read as military records

The northern lists count warriors, give totals and speak of "bands ready for war." On this reading they come from census or army rolls, perhaps David's (21:1–6; 27:23–24), and the Chronicler used what he had, which explains why some tribes are full and others missing.
Read as the north remembered

The northern kingdom had been gone for three centuries when Chronicles was written. On this reading the chapter's purpose is to keep the north in Israel's family: the Chronicler refuses to let the tribes of Samaria be forgotten, even when he has only scraps.

views.H: Traditional readers take the lists as records of the northern tribes kept from the time of David. The story of Ephraim's sons was read as an event before the exodus.
views.C: Critical scholars see damage and gaps in the chapter: Zebulun and Dan missing, a confused Manasseh section (7:14–15), and perhaps a misplaced Benjamin list. The Ephraim story likely preserves a tradition of Ephraimites living in Canaan without going down to Egypt.
views.S: Nothing here comes from Samuel–Kings. The names come largely from Genesis 46, Numbers 26 and Joshua 16–17, with others from unknown sources. The note that Manasseh's cities included Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo and Dor (7:29) differs from Judges 1:27, which says Manasseh did not take them.
views.J: The Talmud tells of Ephraimites who left Egypt early and were killed by the men of Gath, and says God led Israel away from the Philistine road so they would not see the bones (Bavli Sanhedrin 92b). Serah daughter of Asher became a legend of long life.
views.X: Revelation 7:5–8 lists twelve tribes of the redeemed, leaving out Dan, as this chapter seems to. Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus suggested Dan was omitted because the Antichrist would come from Dan.

echoes: Genesis 46:13–25; Numbers 26:23–51; Numbers 27:1–11; Joshua 16:1–17:18; Judges 1:27–29; Judges 6:11; Genesis 37:34–35; Revelation 7:5–8

settings.by: The Chronicler, from tribal and military lists
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud)
settings.when: Written after the return from Babylon (most scholars: about 400–300 BC)
settings.why: Issachar, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Asher and Benjamin are listed even though most of the northern tribes had been lost for centuries. Including them told readers that 'all Israel' still meant the tribes of the north, and that northerners belonged to the family. The lists are not complete: Zebulun is missing, and Dan appears at most as 'Hushim' (7:12). Benjamin's long list leads to Saul's family, setting up the story that follows.

title: Benjamin and the House of Saul
sum: Benjamin's line is given a second time, more fully than in 7:6–12. Its clans lived at Geba, in Moab, at Ono and Lod, at Aijalon and in Jerusalem. One family was carried off to Manahath; another drove out the people of Gath. A man named Shaharaim had sons in Moab after sending away two wives.

The chapter ends with Saul's family at Gibeon: Ner, Kish, Saul, Jonathan, Merib-baal and Micah, then about ten more generations after Micah, down to the archers of Ulam with their 150 sons and grandsons. The first king lost his kingdom, but his family was still part of Israel, living in Jerusalem beside their kin.
readings: Read as Benjamin's records

Benjamin, with Judah and Levi, was one of the three tribes that made up the returned community. Its long list reflects that: these were the readers' own families, with ties to towns resettled after the exile, like Ono and Lod (Ezra 2:33).
Read as a bridge to Saul

On this reading the chapter leads to Saul's story in chapter 10. Saul's house is traced with care and respect, even to generations long after him. The Chronicler will not tell Saul's reign, only his death (10:1–14), but he gives Saul's family its full place in Israel.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as the register of Benjamin's families, ending with Saul's descendants into the time of the exile.
views.C: Critical scholars see a collection of Benjaminite lists of various dates, some linked to places important after the exile. The Saul genealogy, repeated in 9:35–44, may come from a family record of Saul's descendants in Jerusalem.
views.S: Samuel calls Saul's son Ish-bosheth and Jonathan's son Mephibosheth; Chronicles keeps the older forms Esh-baal and Merib-baal. It makes Ner Saul's grandfather, while 1 Samuel 14:51 seems to make him Saul's uncle. Samuel lists only some of Saul's sons and nothing after Mica (2 Samuel 9:12).
views.J: The rabbis noticed that Mordecai's family tree ends with "Kish, a Benjaminite" (Esther 2:5) and connected him with Saul's house: the family that spared Agag later defeated Haman the Agagite (Bavli Megillah 13a). Jonathan's love for David became the model of love that does not depend on gain (Mishnah Avot 5:16).
views.X: The apostle Paul, "of the tribe of Benjamin" and named after Israel's first king (Philippians 3:5; Acts 13:21), came from this tribe. Christian readers have seen in Saul's line continuing a sign of God's mercy to a fallen house.

echoes: Genesis 46:21; Numbers 26:38–41; Judges 3:15; Judges 20:16; 1 Samuel 9:1; 1 Samuel 14:49–51; 2 Samuel 2:8; 2 Samuel 9:1–13; Ezra 2:33; Philippians 3:5

title: Home from Exile
sum: The genealogies end where they were going: "All Israel" was enrolled, Judah was exiled to Babylon for unfaithfulness, and some came back. The first inhabitants listed in Jerusalem came from Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim and Manasseh, with priests, Levites and temple servants (9:1–16). The list is close to Nehemiah 11, with differences in names and numbers.

The gatekeepers get most of the space: their families, their history back to the wilderness and Phinehas, their posts appointed by David and Samuel, their week-long shifts, the keys they kept and the rooms they guarded (9:17–27). Others counted the utensils, kept the flour, oil and spices, baked the cakes and set out the bread each Sabbath, and the singers sang day and night (9:28–34). Saul's family is repeated (9:35–44) to bring the reader to Saul's death in chapter 10.
readings: Read as the returned community

On this reading 9:2–34 describes Jerusalem after the exile, in the Chronicler's own time or earlier. The returned community is small but complete: all Israel is represented, the priests and Levites are in place, and the temple's daily round goes on. The genealogies have led from Adam to the readers themselves.
Read as the ideal temple

Others read the chapter as a picture of how the temple should run, set against the time of David and Samuel (9:22). Its careful division of tasks, its guards around the clock and its unbroken song describe worship as it ought to be, a pattern the rest of Chronicles will show kings keeping or breaking.

views.H: Traditional readers take 9:2–34 as the list of the first settlers after the return under Zerubbabel, parallel to Nehemiah's list of a later time.
views.C: Critical scholars generally see 9:2–34 as related to Nehemiah 11, either drawn from it or from a common source, and updated with the Chronicler's emphasis on the Levites and gatekeepers. Mentioning Ephraim and Manasseh in Jerusalem (9:3) reflects the Chronicler's "all Israel" outlook.
views.S: 9:1 gives the reason for the exile, unfaithfulness, in the Chronicler's own word; Kings gives the same verdict at length (2 Kings 17:7–23; 24:3–4). 9:35–44 repeats 8:29–38 as a lead-in to the story of Saul's death, which Chronicles takes from 1 Samuel 31.
views.J: The rabbis identified the temple servants (9:2) with the Gibeonites (Bavli Yevamot 79a). The Mishnah describes the gatekeepers' and priests' night watch and the opening of the gates at dawn (Mishnah Tamid 1:1; Middot 1:1).
views.X: The priestly shifts continue in Luke 1:5–9, where Zechariah serves in his division. The singers' praise "day and night" (9:33) is echoed in the worship around God's throne (Revelation 4:8), and the church's tradition of daily prayer has drawn on it.

deep.b:
Readers often skip 1 Chronicles 1–9. The writer clearly thought them worth the space. Scholars point to several purposes.

Identity. After the exile, belonging to Israel meant being in the family registers. Priests who could not find their records were barred from service (Ezra 2:59–63). The genealogies are the community's charter.

All Israel. Every tribe appears, including the lost northern tribes, even when the writer has only fragments (7:12–13). For the Chronicler Israel is still twelve tribes, though few came back.

Continuity. The lines run from Adam through the exile to the returned community. The readers are the same people God chose.

David and Levi at the center. Judah, with David's line, comes first and is longest; Levi stands in the middle; Benjamin, Saul's tribe, ends the list. The arrangement anticipates the book's subject: the kingdom of David and the temple worship he set up.

Life inside the lists. Short stories break in: Er's death (2:3), Achar's sin (2:7), Jabez's prayer (4:9–10), Simeon's raids (4:38–43), the eastern tribes' war (5:18–22), Ephraim's grief (7:21–24). Each one teaches the book's lesson in miniature: faithfulness brings blessing, unfaithfulness brings loss.

echoes: Nehemiah 11:3–24; Ezra 2:36–63; Numbers 3:5–10; Numbers 25:7–13; Exodus 30:22–38; Leviticus 24:5–9; Psalm 134:1; Luke 1:8–9; Revelation 4:8

settings.what: The people who came back to Jerusalem
settings.by: The Chronicler, using a list like Nehemiah 11
settings.to: The Jews of Judah after the exile (Yehud), who could find their families here
settings.why: The genealogies end with 'Israel' living in Jerusalem again: people of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh, priests, Levites and gatekeepers. This is the readers' own community. Placing them right before the story of David says that the restored people are the heirs of everything that follows.
